clue.text: Who'll get over first depends on it

definitions.text: Who'll get over first depends on it

parts.words: Who'll get over first depends on it
parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six balls; the list deciding which batsman goes in first and in what sequence settles who faces the first over

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what decides who will be first to scramble over an obstacle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' reads as climbing across something, but it is the cricket term for six deliveries, and the list that fixes which batsmen go in when is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket team's lineup list fixes which batsman walks out to the crease first, second and so on.

clue.text: Scottish surprise at the contents of the cheese roll

indicators.note: the exclamation becomes what is held inside the cheese, the filling of its middle

parts.note: Brie is a soft French cheese
och is a Scots exclamation of surprise or regret

explanation.surface: A Scot exclaims in surprise at what is inside a cheese roll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheese roll' looks like one sandwich, but the cheese is BRIE holding OCH, and 'roll' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A brioche is a soft sweet bread bun, a kind of roll.

parts.note: read 'draws' as 'ties' in a contest, so the man is one who ties; and a bank of seats or oars is a row, a layer rising above another

explanation.surface: A man withdraws money from his bank account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draws from the bank' suggests cash withdrawal; instead 'draws' means ties a match, and a bank is a rank or row.
explanation.definitionFit: One who ties a game draws it, and a row in a rising bank of seats is a layer of the same name.

parts.note: speaking in musical tones, chanting words on a level pitch, as a priest does in church

explanation.surface: Someone expresses their feelings through song rather than speech.
explanation.definitionFit: To chant words in a sing-song voice is to recite them in musical tones.

definitions.meaning: a secret is revealed and spreads

explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb covers both escaping a place and a secret leaking into public knowledge.

definitions.meaning: a deep red colour, also the gemstone

explanation.definitionFit: Ruby is a given name for girls and also a deep crimson shade, like the gemstone.

parts.note: a turn is a performer's act, so repeat performances demanded by an audience are turns given again

explanation.surface: Something rotates once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turns' looks like rotating; it is the noun for a stage act.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra performances called for by an applauding audience are repeated stage acts.

parts.note: 'dish' is slang for an attractive person, and this one is wet from swimming

explanation.surface: A soggy plate or a watery meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dish' suggests food or crockery; it is slang for a good-looking person, here one fresh from the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: An attractive swimsuit-clad person at the beach or pool, such as in a seaside contest.

clue.text: Did they charge a stiff price for their wares?

definitions.text: Did they charge a stiff price for their wares?

parts.words: Did they charge a stiff price for their wares?
parts.note: a 'stiff' is slang for a corpse; grave robbers sold dug-up cadavers to anatomists

explanation.surface: A question about traders who overcharged for their goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stiff price' means a high price, but a stiff is a corpse: these traders sold dead bodies to medical schools.
explanation.definitionFit: Resurrection men stole corpses from graves to sell for dissection in the 18th and 19th centuries.

indicators.note: the insect eats, so it takes the green shade into its middle

parts.note: an ant is a small insect
lime is a shade of green

explanation.surface: A green bug is eating its food.
explanation.definitionFit: Aliment is a formal word for nourishment or sustenance.

clue.text: Leaves wrapped up to be burnt

definitions.text: Leaves wrapped up to be burnt

parts.words: Leaves wrapped up to be burnt
parts.note: dried plant leaves rolled in paper or into cigars and smoked

explanation.surface: Fallen autumn foliage is bundled up for a bonfire.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests garden leaves on a bonfire; these are the dried leaves rolled into cigars and cigarettes.
explanation.definitionFit: Cigars and cigarettes are dried leaves of a plant rolled up and set alight for smoking.

definitions.meaning: a horse kept for ordinary riding or hire

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a hired riding horse and to chop crudely and roughly.

clue.text: Above all, not going out to work

indicators.note: the word not goes out of its usual form, its letters shifted into a new order

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: Most of all, someone refuses to leave home for their job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not going out' reads as staying home; here 'going out' is the anagram signal, and 'to' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Being uppermost or in addition to everything else means being placed at the summit.

parts.note: an old-fashioned courteous request, as when asking a gentleman politely to do something

explanation.surface: Someone sets out to satisfy a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Please' looks like a verb meaning to gratify; it is the polite word of request, as in an archaic plea to a gentleman.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic word for 'please' in requests, as in asking someone kindly to be seated.

parts.note: 'meal' here is ground grain, the powder used in baking

explanation.surface: Someone eats dinner at the kitchen table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meal' suggests dinner; it is ground grain, the baker's powder.
explanation.definitionFit: Finely ground wheat is a kind of meal kept in every kitchen for baking.

clue.text: Bilingual article on the cause of amnesia

parts.note: le is the French definite article
the is the English definite article

explanation.surface: A piece of writing in two languages about memory loss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bilingual article' is not a two-language essay but the word for 'the' in two languages, French and English.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the river of the underworld whose waters made the dead forget their past lives.

definitions.meaning: things that jab, sharp points that prick

explanation.definitionFit: Sewing pins and syringe points prick, and to goad someone with persistent annoyance has the same name.

clue.text: At a loss to rationalise the disloyalty

indicators.note: the word at suffers the loss of its own A, leaving only one letter behind

parts.note: to rationalise is to reason something out

explanation.surface: Someone cannot explain away an act of betrayal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At a loss' reads as bewildered; split, it says AT loses A, leaving T.
explanation.definitionFit: Betrayal of one's country or sovereign is the gravest form of disloyalty.

parts.note: a light brown shade shares its name with the crunchy treat dogs love

explanation.surface: A whimsical question about which shade a pet dog prefers.
explanation.walkthrough: Dogs love the treat, and the same word names a pale yellowish-brown colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A pale brown shade named after the baked treat, which dogs are famously fond of.

indicators.note: the abbreviation sits inside the dog breed's name

parts.note: a setter is a breed of gun dog

explanation.surface: A colonist speaking mock Latin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog Latin' is mock Latin, but here the dog is a SETTER with L placed inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who settles in a new land is a colonist or pioneer.

indicators.note: the word trained done badly, its letters scrambled out of order

explanation.surface: A poorly trained animal is exchanged for a different one.
explanation.definitionFit: To hand over an old item as part-payment for a new one is to exchange it.

clue.text: Can I turn her in and get the money?

indicators.note: the female pronoun is placed inside the turned can
the word for a can is turned round to run the opposite way

parts.note: a tin is a can

explanation.surface: Someone schemes to hand a woman over to the police and collect a reward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn her in' reads as betraying a woman to the police; 'turn' actually acts on the can alone, and 'in' does the containing.
explanation.definitionFit: To receive a legacy from a relative's will is to come into their wealth.

clue.text: The great difficulty is I have gone past my prime

parts.note: I'm can stand for 'I have' less often than 'I am'; here it gives the contraction
passé means faded or past one's best

explanation.surface: Someone laments that their best years are behind them.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as I'M PASSÉ: 'I am past it'.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadlock or dead end is a situation with no way forward, a great difficulty.

clue.text: Ruled it must be checked aloud

indicators.note: the word for being checked is spoken, and its sound gives a different spelling

parts.note: a horse that is reined is checked or restrained

explanation.surface: Something was decided and must now be verified out loud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'checked' means restrained with reins, giving REINED, which sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch who held the throne governed or ruled the realm.

clue.text: As a cockney, stop at nothing to become a singer

indicators.note: cockneys famously drop their initial aitches, so the word loses its H

parts.note: to halt is to stop
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A Londoner will stop at nothing to achieve fame as a vocalist.
explanation.walkthrough: A cockney is a working-class Londoner whose accent drops the H at the start of words. 'Stop at nothing' looks like ruthless ambition; it is HALT, dropped H, then O.
explanation.definitionFit: A singer with a low female or high male voice, the part below soprano.

clue.text: Is no longer an addition to the hazards of summer

parts.note: is put into the past becomes was
a PS, postscript, is an addition to a letter

explanation.surface: Something is no longer an extra danger of the warm season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is no longer' gives the past tense WAS; a PS is a postscript, an addition to a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Stinging insects buzzing around picnics are a familiar summertime nuisance.

parts.note: to ask for something while dropping a coin in a well

explanation.surface: A request phrased with careful eloquence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well-chosen' looks like 'carefully picked'; split it, and the words are chosen at a well, a wishing well.
explanation.definitionFit: To desire something and voice it, as when throwing a coin into a wishing well.

parts.note: the lowest male singing voice, and also a fish caught on a fishing line

explanation.surface: Someone's voice heard down a telephone line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line' suggests a phone line; it is a fishing line, with the fish named like the deepest voice.
explanation.definitionFit: The deepest male singing voice shares its name with a fish an angler hooks.

clue.text: Game that only you can play?

definitions.text: Game that only you can play?

parts.words: Game that only you can play?
parts.note: a card game (a whist variant) whose name also means performed alone

explanation.surface: A question about a game for a single player.
explanation.walkthrough: It is a whist variant, and the word also means a performance by one person alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A whist-type card game shares its name with a performance by one person alone.

parts.note: till means up to, as in 'till dawn'
an age is a long time

explanation.surface: The foundations are laid in good time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Groundwork' looks like preparation; it is literal work on the ground, ploughing.
explanation.definitionFit: Ploughing and cultivating land for crops is literally work done on the ground.

clue.text: He made the round sum sound rum

definitions.text: He made the round sum sound rum

parts.words: He made the round sum sound rum
parts.note: the Oxford don famed for swapping the initial sounds of words, so 'round sum' came out as 'sound rum'

explanation.surface: Someone made a tidy total seem odd.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue itself performs the slip it names: swap the first sounds of 'round sum' and you get 'sound rum', rum being British slang for odd.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oxford don William Archibald gave his name to the slip of swapping first sounds of words.

parts.note: 'time' is slang for a jail sentence, so this is a list of the jail sentences someone has served

explanation.surface: A schedule of times, like a train timetable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doing time' means serving a jail sentence, so a table of someone's time is a list of their convictions.
explanation.definitionFit: A list of a criminal's past convictions and sentences served behind bars.
